_: Tuesday's case (Jay, 2026-10-24). Dame Margot Fenn's supper for forty years on the stage; the lights go out at the chicken and when they come back her rival is dead. Source of services/hubs/src/lounge/mysteries/tue.json (mystery-script.py).
title: LIGHTS OUT: WHO KILLED CLAUDIA DEVERE?

switch.text: The lights were switched off, not blown

gloves.text: Something white moved behind the chairs in the dark

syringe.text: A syringe from the doctor's bag

insulin.text: Albert gives Margot her injections every night

secret.text: Claudia knew a secret about Toby's father

play.text: Claudia laughed at Toby's play in the papers

lines: Forty years. Forty years on the stage, and tonight I don't have to learn a single line. Isn't it heaven?
You look exactly as you did in nineteen twenty three, Margot. In Private Lives.
I was dreadful in Private Lives, Hugh. Noel said so. Noel said so in print.
Noel says that about everybody, darling. It's how he says hello.
Claudia. You came. How brave of you.
I wouldn't miss your farewell for anything, Margot. I've been waiting for it for years.
Mother, the Major's brought you a present. It ticks. I think it's a clock, but I'd stand back.
It's a carriage clock, Toby. For a woman who has never once been on time.
Hugh, I'm touched. I shall keep it in a drawer, where it can't see me.
And I know every pill. Margot, did you take your evening dose?
Albert gave it to me at six, Simon. Albert never forgets.
In, everybody. Hugh, your arm. Toby, take Claudia in, and try not to argue with her before the soup.
I never argue with Claudia. I simply disagree with everything she says.
That's arguing, Toby. They teach it at Cambridge.
Thank you, Doctor. Mind the step. Everybody minds the step but nobody ever sees it.
Sit, sit. Albert hates people standing about. It upsets his arrangements.
Glasses up, darlings. To forty years. To every theatre that's ever had me, and every critic who never will again.
Now. For our two friends in the middle, who don't know any of these people. I'll do the honours, I always do.
Major Hugh Bramwell. My oldest friend. He spent the war in intelligence, which is to say he spent it in a basement, being very clever in a whisper.
My son, Toby. A playwright. His last play ran for a week.
Nine days. Mother never counts the matinees.
Miss Claudia Devere. My understudy for the last five years. She's played my part twice, when I had the flu, and she's never let me forget it.
The notices were very kind, darling. Kinder than they've been to you.
Doctor Simon Okafor. My doctor. He keeps me alive for a living, and sends a very large bill for it.
Miss Lucy March. My dresser. She has sewn me into every costume I've worn since the war.
And Albert. Albert has been with me thirty one years. Butler, chauffeur, and the only man who has never once let me down.
Asparagus, Toby. Just like your play. Long, thin, and nobody quite knew what to do with it.
You never saw my play, Claudia.
I read the notices, darling. I read all of them. Out loud. At the Ivy.
She must, Toby. She's an actress. They must everything.
Margot, is it true? You're really finished? No more first nights?
No more first nights, Hugh. The Haymarket is reviving Hedda Gabler in the spring, and for the first time in thirty years, I shan't be Hedda.
Hasn't it? I'd heard it had.
Miss Devere, the green suits you. It always did.
You'd know, Lucy. You used to steam it for me. Before you went to Dame Margot.
Before you dismissed me, Miss Devere.
Over a brooch, darling. You borrowed a brooch. It was in all the papers.
It was in one paper. And I gave it back.
Leave Lucy alone, Claudia. Lucy's mine now. Nobody is unkind to my dresser but me.
Doctor, is it true Mother's diabetic? She tells everybody but she won't tell me.
Since nineteen fifty, Toby. Insulin, every evening. It's no secret.
It's not a secret, darling. It's simply nobody's business.
Albert does her injections. Don't you, Albert? Every night at six. Behind a locked door.
Madam's injections are madam's business, miss.
Albert has the steadiest hands in London. Steadier than mine. I trained him myself.
You did, Simon. In nineteen fifty. He practised on an orange for a month. We had marmalade until Easter.
Albert, is that true? An orange?
Several oranges, Master Toby. And a grapefruit, for the difficult days.
Margot, I'm writing my memoirs. Did I mention?
You mentioned it at the door, Claudia, and in the lift, and on the terrace.
Chapter nine is about this flat. And about the summer of nineteen thirty five.
Nobody wants to read about nineteen thirty five, Claudia. It was a very dull year.
Not for you, darling. You were away for six months. Switzerland, wasn't it? For your chest.
I was born in nineteen thirty five. In Switzerland. Mother says the air was very good for me.
Oh, I know, Toby. I know all about where you came from.
Miss Devere, I think that's quite enough about Switzerland.
Do you, Major? I think it's only the beginning.
Margot, your colour. Are you all right?
Perfectly all right, Simon. It's the asparagus. It always makes me want to kill somebody.
Mister Toby, will there be a new play? After the last one?
There's always a new play, Lucy. It's what playwrights have instead of money.
There's always a new play, and there's always a new bank manager.
At least I write my own lines, Claudia.
Darling, I improve other people's. It's much harder.
Albert, is there more of the white? It's very good.
There is, sir. The waiters will bring it with the fish.
The soup, madam. Pea and mint.
Thank you, Albert. Everybody eat. Lucy, eat. You're thinner than my last review.
I'm always thin when you're nervous, Dame Margot.
I'm never nervous, Lucy. I'm an actress. I'm simply alert.
I telephoned the Haymarket today, Margot. About the spring. They said you'd recommended someone for Hedda.
Did they, Simon. How very indiscreet of them.
Have you recommended someone, Margot? Have you?
I've recommended a girl from Bristol, Claudia. She's twenty three and she can cry on cue.
You cry on cue, darling. She cries when it matters.
You'll change your mind. You'll change it before the spring. I know you will.
I never change my mind, Claudia. I only change my costume.
Major, were you really in intelligence? What did you do?
I listened, Toby. For six years I sat in a basement in Bletchley with a pair of earphones and a very cold cup of tea, and listened.
To people lying, mostly. You get an ear for it. It never quite goes away.
How awkward for you, Major. At dinner parties.
Very awkward, Miss Devere. Especially tonight.
Albert, did you bring Dame Margot's shawl up from the car? She'll want it later.
It's in the hall, Miss March. With the doctor's bag and the Major's umbrella. Everything is where it should be.
Albert. The fuses. They've been doing that all week.
It's the building, madam. They're rewiring the floor below. I'll stand by the switch, in case.
Albert's always standing by something of Margot's. Aren't you, Albert? Thirty one years.
I stand where madam needs me, miss.
Margot, if the lights go, nobody move. I don't want anyone breaking a hip on my account. I'd have to set it.
Simon, darling, if the lights go, I'll be the one sitting quite still in the dark, enjoying the rest.
Toby, what's your middle name? I've known you thirty years and I've never asked.
Albert. Tobias Albert Fenn. Mother named me after the butler. She says he's the only man who never let her down.
It's true, Hugh. It was either Albert or Noel, and Noel would have charged me for it.
Margot, darling, I'll be frank. I want Hedda.
I know you do, Claudia. You've wanted every part I've ever had, including the husband.
I could have had the husband. I didn't want him. Reginald wore spats.
Reginald was a very kind man.
Reginald was a very kind man in spats, darling. There's a limit.
Why don't you leave her alone? It's her night. It's her party.
Because, Toby, I've left her alone for five years, standing in the wings, while she coughed through Ibsen. Now it's my turn.
Darling. I don't audition. I negotiate.
Dame Margot, the Haymarket. Is it really the girl from Bristol?
It's really the girl from Bristol, Lucy. I saw her Rosalind in Bath. She made me cry, and I hadn't cried since the Coronation.
Margot cried at the Coronation because she wasn't asked to read anything.
I cried because the Queen looked so tired, Claudia. And she had to be nice to Noel.
You two in the middle are very quiet. Clever. Never say anything at a theatrical supper. They'll put it in a play.
I've never put anyone in a play, Major.
Oh, Toby. Darling. Your last one was entirely about your mother. The lead had a son with no father.
It was a confession, darling. Just not yours.
Ask your mother, Toby. At the cheese. Mothers always tell the truth at the cheese.
The fish, madam. Cod, with a parsley sauce.
Thank you, Albert. Cod. How very honest.
Claudia, you said something earlier. About my wife. I'd rather you didn't.
Did I, Simon? I'm sure I didn't mean anything. I never mean anything at supper.
You never mean anything anywhere, Claudia. That's what frightens people.
Miss Devere, you seem to know something about everybody at this table.
I'm an understudy, Major. Understudies watch. For five years I've stood in the wings and watched. You'd be amazed what you see from the wings.
I spent six years in a basement listening. I can imagine.
Then we're the same, Major. Except that I'm going to be paid for it.
Mother, what happened in Switzerland? She keeps saying it like it's a joke I'm not in on.
Nothing happened in Switzerland, Toby. You were born, and the air was very good, and we came home.
And my father? He died in nineteen thirty six. You always say. A riding accident.
A riding accident, darling. A very brave man on a very stupid horse.
Very brave. Very stupid. Very conveniently dead. Wasn't he, Albert?
I couldn't say, miss. I wasn't there.
Weren't you, Albert? I've seen the photographs. Montreux, nineteen thirty five. You were driving.
Margot. Is everything quite all right?
Everything is perfectly all right, Hugh. Claudia has had three glasses of champagne and she's rehearsing her memoirs.
Chapter nine, darling. It's going to be wonderful.
My bag. I left my bag in the hall. Is that safe, Margot? There's insulin in it, and syringes.
Everything in my hall is safe, Simon. Albert sees to it.
Your bag is on the chair by the umbrellas, sir. Nobody has touched it but me.
To move it, sir. Off the hall table, where the coats go.
Toby, darling, read us something. From your new play. I'm dying to hear it.
You're not dying to hear anything, Claudia. You're dying to laugh.
Both, darling. I can do both. I trained.
You wrote in the Express that my last play was the first tragedy in history in which only the audience died.
It was a very good line, Toby. You should have written it.
Claudia, that was cruel, and you know it. He was twenty six.
I was twenty six once, Margot. Somebody was cruel to me. It was you, in the Telegraph, in nineteen fifty.
I said you had a lovely speaking voice.
You said I had a lovely speaking voice for radio.
Doctor, what's in insulin that makes it dangerous? I've always wondered.
Nothing, if you need it, Major. If you don't, a large dose drops the blood sugar like a stone. Confusion. Collapse. And then you don't wake up.
Into a vein, very quickly. A minute, perhaps. Why do you ask?
I'm a nosy old man, Doctor. It's all I've got left.
Dame Margot, shall I fetch your biscuit? You look pale.
Albert has my biscuit, Lucy. In his waistcoat. Albert has everything I need.
Isn't it sweet? Thirty one years. Albert has everything she needs. Albert drives her. Albert dresses her wounds. Albert even gives her injections.
You've been very loyal, Albert. Very loyal indeed. More loyal than a butler has any need to be.
It wasn't a compliment, Albert. It was a question. We'll come back to it.
Margot, I really think you should eat something. Your hands are shaking.
My hands are shaking because I'm sitting next to a woman writing a book about me, Simon. It isn't my sugar.
Major, you knew my father, didn't you? Before the horse?
I met him once, Toby. At the races. He was very charming and he didn't know a thing about horses.
Margot, I'll be honest. If I have Hedda, there's no chapter nine. I'll never write it. I'll be far too busy being brilliant.
And if you don't have Hedda?
Then I'll have Thursday at the Ivy, darling, with my publisher, and a very good lunch.
Mango. How exotic. Albert, you're spoiling us.
Miss Devere, you can't. You can't put her in a book. Not after forty years.
Forty years is precisely why, Lucy. Nobody wants to read about a beginner.
You're a horrible woman. I always thought so. Even when I steamed your green.
Thank you, Lucy. I'll put that in chapter four.
Miss Devere, do you have it written down? This chapter nine?
Oh, Major. I don't need it written down. It's all up here. And in a letter to my publisher, in a safe, in Fleet Street. I'm not a fool.
No. I don't think anybody here thinks you're a fool.
Excuse me. I must check my bag. My wife may have telephoned the porter.
Sit down, Simon. If your wife had telephoned, Albert would have told you. Albert hears telephones in his sleep.
Claudia. What do you want? Really? Not Hedda. What do you actually want?
I want to be Dame Claudia, Toby. And I want your mother to hand me the part herself, in front of everybody, at her own party.
Then everybody finds out who your father was.
Claudia. After the chicken. We'll talk. Privately.
We'll talk now, Margot. I've waited five years. I'm not waiting for a chicken.
Oh. Please. In five years you've never said please to me. I'm going to remember this.
Margot, shall I take Miss Devere for a little walk on the terrace? Some air?
No, Hugh. Let her sit. Let her have her supper. She's earned it, standing in my wings.
Albert, Dame Margot needs her biscuit. Now, please. Look at her.
Not that. Forgive me, madam. That's tomorrow's.
Oh, Albert. Not at the table. Put it away.
The biscuit is in the other pocket, madam. I'm sorry. It's been a long evening.
You carry madam's syringe about with you, Albert?
Always, sir. In case. You told me so yourself, in nineteen fifty.
I did. I did, didn't I.
Major, you're watching everybody. Like a cat.
Bletchley, Toby. A man who's listened to lies for six years never really stops. It's terribly bad for dinner parties.
I'd like to make a speech. At the chicken. For Margot. A little tribute.
I will, darling. I've written it. It's very moving. There's a part about Switzerland.
Claudia, if you stand up with that speech, I'll never speak to you again.
You've never spoken to me, Margot. You've spoken at me, for five years, from the stage.
Margot, let her. Let everyone hear it. Things are always worse said in the dark.
Hugh, you have no idea what you're saying.
I spent six years listening, Margot. I generally know what I'm saying.
Doctor, is Dame Margot all right? She's very white.
Her sugar, Lucy. And Claudia. Neither is good for her.
Margot, eat something. Anything. A bread roll.
I'll eat at the chicken, Simon. I'll need my strength for the chicken.
The chicken, madam. Roasted, with tarragon.
And now, while we've all got our chicken. My speech.
Claudia, sit down. Please. I'm asking you.
Forty years ago, a girl from Harrogate stepped onto a stage in a borrowed frock and stole a play from under the nose of the leading lady. That girl was Margot Fenn.
Thank you, Major. And twenty five years ago, that girl went to Switzerland for her chest, and came back with a son. And a very loyal chauffeur.
I won't stop it, Toby. I'm the understudy. It's my job to know the lines when the star can't say them.
Miss Devere, sit down. You've had a great deal of champagne.
I've had exactly enough, Major. Any less and I'd be polite.
Where was I? Switzerland. The air. The chest. The chauffeur, waiting in the car with the engine running, every single night.
Beg, darling. You do it so beautifully. You did it to the Haymarket every spring for thirty years.
And so, to Margot. To forty years. And to Toby's father, who is with us tonight, in a manner of speaking.
Nobody move! Nobody move, you'll break something!
I can't see my hands. I can't see anything.
Stay in your seats. All of you. Stay exactly where you are.
Who's that? Somebody's moving. I heard a chair.
There's something. Behind the chairs. Something white.
All present. Nobody hurt. Claudia? Claudia, you can stop now. The lights are back.
Let me see her. Major, I'm a doctor.
Stay where you are, Doctor. She's past doctors.
She's dead. She's dead, isn't she.
She's dead, Lucy. There's a mark on her neck. A pinprick. Just here.
Murder, Margot. In the dark. At your table.
Murder? She had a heart attack. She was shouting, she was drinking...
Hearts don't leave a pinprick, Toby. Somebody walked round this table in the dark and put a needle in her neck.
A needle. Good God. My bag.
Your bag, Doctor. In the hall. With the insulin and the syringes.
I haven't left this table since the soup! You all saw me!
Nobody saw anything for eighteen seconds, Doctor. That's rather the point.
Albert. Telephone the police. And bring the doctor's bag from the hall. Don't open it.
Major, I saw something. In the dark. Behind the chairs on the other side. Something white. Moving.
Like a glove. Like a pair of gloves. Going round, very fast and very quiet.
You two in the middle. One of you was right by her. Somebody walked behind your chair in the dark, didn't they? You'd have felt it.
There's a board at the end of the table. Put your pins on whoever you think it was. Change your mind as often as you like. When the pudding comes, it closes.
The police are coming, sir. The bag, sir. It was open, on the chair by the umbrellas. One syringe gone from the case. I found it in the umbrella stand.
That's mine. That's one of mine. The case is mine.
You found it in the umbrella stand, Albert. In the dark hall. In half a minute.
I have good eyes, sir. For my age.
You do, Albert. Keep it in your pocket, where I can see the shape of it. And go back to your switch.
Doctor. Your bag. Did anyone know what was in it?
Everybody knew. Margot's insulin. I said so at the fish. I said it to the whole table.
You did. And a syringe of insulin, into a vein, would do exactly what we saw.
In a minute. Perhaps less. But I'll tell you something, Major. A layman couldn't find a vein in the dark. Not in a neck. Not in eighteen seconds.
A doctor could. Or a nurse. Or anyone who'd done it every night for years.
Major, I'll be frank too. Claudia and I. Two years ago. Briefly. She's been writing to my wife.
Nothing, yet. She sends a blank card every Christmas. My wife thinks it's a joke. I know it's a warning.
The cheese, madam. Brie, with grapes and walnuts.
Thank you, Albert. I don't think anybody wants cheese.
I want cheese, Albert. Murder makes me hungry. It always did. Thank you.
Excuse me, all of you. Toby, keep everybody in their seats. I want to look at something in the hall.
Major, you said nobody leaves the table.
Nobody but me, Toby. Rank has its privileges.
I need a drink. Somebody. Anything.
The white, Margot. Not the brandy. Not with your sugar.
Simon, if I want brandy at my own murder, I'll have brandy.
It's my party, Simon. Everything at it is mine.
Thank you. Nobody moved, I hope.
Albert. The lights. The fuses have gone all week, you said.
I've just been out to the hall. I looked at the fuse box. Every fuse is perfect. Nothing blew tonight.
The switch, Margot. By the door. Somebody switched the lights off, and eighteen seconds later, somebody switched them on again.
But Albert was by the switch. All evening. Mother asked him to stand there, in case.
He was, Toby. Albert has stood by that switch since the soup.
I did, sir. And when the lights went, I went to the table. To madam. In case she fell.
And then I came back and found the switch, sir. It took me a moment. In the dark.
Major. Tell me. About my father. If you know, tell me. I'm thirty one years old.
I'd rather your mother told you, Toby.
I can't. I can't, darling. I've never said it out loud.
Dame Margot, shall I get you your biscuit? Albert, the biscuit.
Thank you, Albert. Thirty one years, and you've never once forgotten my biscuit.
Major, one thing. The mark on her neck. Did you see where it was?
Just below the ear, Doctor. On the left.
Left. Then whoever did it stood behind her and to her left. Right handed. Reaching over the chair back. That's not a stab in the dark. That's a nurse. Or someone trained by one.
Or someone trained by a doctor.
Albert. Your gloves. You've worn white gloves all night.
I always wear them at table, sir. Madam likes it.
Lucy saw something white moving in the dark, behind the chairs, going round the far side of the table. Toward Miss Devere.
Miss March was very frightened, sir. In the dark everybody sees things.
I saw what I saw, Major. I've been in the theatre since I was fourteen. I know what a pair of gloves looks like, moving in the dark. I've watched a hundred stagehands.

An understudy who wanted the part. A son she laughed at in the papers. A dresser she sacked for a brooch. A doctor whose wife gets blank cards at Christmas. And a butler who has stood by the switch for thirty one years.
You two in the middle. The board. You have until the pudding.
Albert. Pour the Major a brandy. And yourself one.
I couldn't, madam. Not at table.
Thirty one years, Albert. Just once. For me.
Later, madam. When the pudding's done.
Lucy, you knew Claudia before. Was she always like this?
Always, Mister Toby. But she was kind to me once. She lent me her coat in the snow in nineteen fifty four. I'd forgotten that until tonight.
Remember it, Lucy. Somebody should remember something kind about her.
The pudding is coming up now, sir.
Pudding. Pins down, please. The board is closed.

Claudia Devere was killed in eighteen seconds of darkness by somebody who walked round this table, behind the chairs, and put a needle of insulin into a vein in her neck, from behind, on the left, without a sound.
The lights were not blown. They were switched off, at the switch by the door, and switched on again eighteen seconds later. Albert was by the switch all evening.
The needle came from the doctor's bag in the hall, and Albert moved that bag tonight, and found the needle again in half a minute, in the dark.
Lucy saw a pair of white gloves going round behind the chairs. Nobody at this table wears gloves.
And there is only one person in this flat who has given an injection every evening for twenty years, and who could find a vein in the dark with his eyes shut.
And Claudia knew who Toby's father was. She was going to say it out loud, at Margot's party, between the chicken and the cheese.
Madam. I'm sorry. I couldn't let her. Not in front of the boy. Not in a book.
Yes, Master Toby. I mean you. I drove your mother to Montreux in the spring of nineteen thirty five. I drove her back in the autumn. With you.
I'm the butler, sir. I've been the butler for thirty one years. It was the best way to be anything at all.
Toby. Darling. I wanted to tell you. Every birthday I wanted to. And every birthday Albert said, not yet, madam. Let the boy have his father on the horse.
There was never a horse, Toby. There was Albert.
Albert, the police will be here directly.
Then I'll wait for them downstairs, sir, if I may. In the hall, by the door. I'd like to put my coat on. I'll not run. Where would I go? Madam's here.
Your biscuit, madam. In my other pocket. Lucy will know which. Goodnight, madam. Goodnight, Toby.
Don't, Lucy. Don't be kind. I've been an actress for forty years. I'll fall down in the morning, on my own, like a professional.
Major. Thank you. I thought for an hour that you'd hang it on me.
I thought about it, Doctor. You had a very good reason. But you were on the wrong side of the table, and you can't find a vein in a hurry. I've seen you try.
Nineteen fifty one. The vicar's wife. She's never forgiven me.
Major. Did you know? All these years?
I guessed, Toby. At your christening. You had his hands. Albert held you like a man holding something he wasn't allowed to keep.
It wasn't mine to say. In Bletchley we had a rule. You only tell a secret to the man it belongs to.
Mister Toby, your middle name. Albert. She named you after him in front of everyone.
In front of everyone. And nobody ever saw it. Not even me.
It was the bravest thing I ever did on any stage, darling. And nobody clapped.
Margot, Claudia's memoirs. The letter in the safe. In Fleet Street.
Let them print it, Simon. Let them print every word. It's true. I've spent thirty one years making sure it wasn't. I'm tired.
You'll have a lot of visitors, Margot. Reporters. Photographers.
Let them come, Hugh. I'll give them the performance of my life. It'll be the first time I've played myself.
You two. In the middle. You were right next to her. Did you feel him go past?
They felt it, Toby. Look at them. Some of them had their pins on him before I'd said a word.
Then you knew before I did. Everybody always knows before I do.
Dame Margot, the girl from Bristol. For Hedda. Is it still her?
It's still her, Lucy. She cries when it matters. We need more people who do.
Mother. When I was nine, I had the measles. Somebody sat up with me every night for a fortnight. I thought it was you.
It was Albert, darling. I was in Manchester. In Mrs Warren's Profession. I telephoned every night at the interval.
He read me Treasure Island. All of it. Twice. He did the voices.
He did Long John Silver very badly. I heard him through the door once. He sounded like a Methodist.
Margot. May I tell them about nineteen twenty three?
I asked her to marry me. In Harrogate, at the stage door, with a ring I'd borrowed from my mother. She said no, because she had a matinee.
It was a very good matinee, Hugh.
It was Juliet, Margot. You were alarming.
I was nineteen. I'm still alarming. Ask the Haymarket.
Dame Margot, I'll do your hair in the morning. Before the reporters. The way you like it for a first night.
Thank you, Lucy. It will be a first night, won't it. The first time I've played the truth.
Then we'll do the good wig. The truth deserves the good wig.
Major, about my wife. The cards. Will it come out? At the trial?
I shouldn't think so, Doctor. Claudia's dead, and dead women send very few cards.
Then I'll tell her myself. On Sunday. Before somebody else does.
That's the bravest thing anybody's said tonight, Doctor. Don't let it go cold.
Major, Claudia's letter. The one in the safe in Fleet Street. Chapter nine.
I'll make a telephone call in the morning, Toby. Bletchley still has a few friends in Fleet Street. Safes are surprisingly easy to lose things from.
Hugh. No. Let them print it. I meant that.
Then I'll ask them to print it properly, Margot. With the right dates. And Albert's name spelled correctly.
You know the worst of it? I'd have liked him for a father. I'd have chosen him. Out of everybody.
You did choose him, darling. Every Christmas, for thirty one years, you gave Albert the best present under the tree. I never knew why.
Neither did I. I just thought he looked lonely in the kitchen.
Will you come to the Haymarket in the spring? To see the girl from Bristol? I'll get you seats. In the stalls. Not the gods.
Come. Please. You've sat through the worst night of my life very politely. You deserve a good one.
Margot, your sugar. You've had nothing since the chicken.
Albert would have had a biscuit, Simon. In his waistcoat.
It's in his other pocket, Dame Margot. He said so on his way out. I'll fetch it from the hall.
No, Lucy. Leave it with him. He'll want something of mine tonight.
I'm a remarkable actress, Hugh. The woman's been rather a disappointment.
Not to me. Not since Harrogate.
Major, will you stay in London? Now that it's over?
As long as your mother needs a man who listens, Toby. I've nothing better to do. I've retired from listening to Germans.
Stay for the spring, Hugh. For the girl from Bristol. Sit in my box and listen to her.
Only if you sit beside me, Margot, and don't mouth the words.
Major, the police will want statements. All of us.
Downstairs, Doctor. In the Rovers. Everybody. I'm not giving a statement anywhere with a dead understudy in it.
Yes. Downstairs. All of you. I want a large brandy, and I want to sit somewhere Albert never stood.
Mother. He'll be in the hall. When we go down.
I know, darling. We'll say goodnight to him properly. Both of us. For the first time.
Come down with us. Please. There's safety in numbers, and we're two short.
